claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy is a single-phase, chemically random solid solution with a homogeneous microstructure.
Demanding mechanical service causes the alloy to lose toughness through stress-assisted, diffusion-mediated chemical ordering or nanoscale phase separation.
Loading produces localized ordered clusters or brittle intermetallic-like domains.
Ordered clusters or domains interrupt homogeneous dislocation motion.
Ordered clusters or domains concentrate strain and act as crack-initiation sites.
Prolonged high, variable, or cyclic loading representative of service is the proposed intervention.
Atomic rearrangement is sufficiently rapid under the proposed 300–600 K service-temperature range and stresses approaching yield.
Loading causes nanometer-scale ordered clusters or incipient brittle precipitates to nucleate and grow in the initially single-phase matrix.
The proposed clusters or precipitates preferentially occur in highly strained regions or near grain or interphase boundaries.
Mechanical loading creates local stress concentrations that enhance atomic diffusion.
Stress-enhanced diffusion drives the formation of chemically ordered regions.
Chemically ordered domains create barriers to slip and reduce homogeneous dislocation motion.
Restricted dislocation motion increases strain localization and crack formation, causing toughness loss or brittle fracture.
Loaded specimens will show more nanoscale ordering or phase separation by TEM, atom-probe tomography, or XRD than unloaded controls.
Loaded specimens will have lower ductility and fracture toughness than unloaded controls.
Loaded specimens will exhibit cleavage facets rather than ductile dimples.
The as-cast, mechanically uncycled baseline has uniform single-phase behavior and higher toughness.
The mechanism applies when temperature, stress, and time provide sufficient atomic mobility without complete recrystallization or melting.
The mechanism is limited at very low temperatures or extremely high strain rates because diffusion is too slow for significant ordering.
The kinetics and critical stress, temperature, and time for the ductile-to-brittle transition vary with alloy composition and processing history.
